title: Premium Video Memberships: Check Personal-Use and Sharing Terms
description: Review subscription terms for personal viewing, household access, account sharing, downloads, and public display before choosing a premium video membership.
excerpt: A membership that gives you viewing access does not automatically explain who may use the account or where content may be shown. Check the written terms against your intended use.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish subscription access from permission to share credentials or show content to others.
Check whether household use, simultaneous viewing, and separate profiles are addressed independently.
Read download and offline-access terms separately from rules about copying or redistribution.
Confirm whether public or business display is excluded or requires separate permission.
Keep a dated copy or note of the applicable terms and ask for clarification when they conflict.

sections.heading: Match the terms to the way you intend to watch
paragraphs: Before joining, describe your intended use in plain terms: watching alone, using an account in a shared household, viewing on multiple devices, or showing content to a group. These scenarios can be treated differently in service terms. A subscription's general promise of access does not, by itself, answer every question about who may use the account or where playback is allowed.

Find the current membership terms, account rules, and any separate content-use or licensing information. Pay attention to definitions such as personal use, household, authorized user, public performance, and redistribution. If the documents use terms that are not defined or appear inconsistent, do not fill the gap with an assumption based on common practice elsewhere. Ask the service for clarification that addresses your actual use case.

sections.heading: Separate account sharing from household viewing
paragraphs: Household access can involve several distinct issues: who is permitted to sign in, whether profiles are available, how many devices may be active, and whether simultaneous playback is allowed. A profile feature may organize viewing without expanding the number of people authorized to use an account. Likewise, a device limit does not necessarily define who may receive account credentials.

Read the relevant rules together rather than relying on a single feature label. If another household member will use the service, check whether the terms expressly cover that situation and whether any profile, access, or device limits apply. Avoid sharing a password as a substitute for a clearly permitted household arrangement. Where allowed account access is ambiguous, request guidance before building a shared routine around the membership.

sections.heading: Do not confuse offline access with copying rights
paragraphs: A download or offline-viewing option, where offered, is a way to access content under the service's stated conditions. It should not be treated as permission to make a separate copy, extract a file, redistribute content, or retain access after the service's stated entitlement ends. Check download availability and expiration rules separately from any restrictions on copying or sharing.

The same distinction applies to screenshots, recordings, or transfers to another device. Unless the terms clearly permit a particular action, do not infer permission from a playback control or a technical ability to capture content. Review the current terms and help documentation for the relevant feature. If you need broader rights than ordinary individual viewing, seek explicit written permission rather than relying on a general membership description.

sections.heading: Check restrictions on public or organizational display
paragraphs: Watching at home and showing material in a workplace, venue, event, or other public setting are different use cases. A service's personal membership may not grant permission for public exhibition or organizational use. Check for terms addressing public display, commercial use, group viewing, or redistribution, and look for whether separate licensing is required.

If the service does not explain your proposed setting, describe it accurately when contacting support. Ask whether the membership covers the audience, location, and purpose you have in mind, and whether any additional permission is needed. Do not assume that a private room, a small audience, or the absence of a direct charge automatically changes the applicable terms. This guide is not legal advice; when the consequences matter, consult a qualified professional about the specific use.

sections.heading: Keep a clear record of the terms you relied on
paragraphs: Terms and account rules can change. Save or note the date you reviewed them, the plan or membership scope, and any written answer from support. If the service presents different rules across its terms, help pages, and account interface, record the conflict and ask which source governs the use you intend. A concise record is more useful than keeping an unorganized set of screenshots.

Revisit the relevant rules if your use changes, such as adding household members, using a new device arrangement, or showing content in a group setting. Do not assume an answer about one situation applies to another. If the service's response is unclear, choose a narrower use that is plainly permitted or delay the activity until the scope is resolved. This reduces the chance of confusing access to a title with permission to use it in a different way.
bullets: Write down the exact use case before contacting support.
Save the date and source of the terms you reviewed.
Keep access, device, download, and public-display questions separate.

faqs.question: Does a subscription automatically let everyone in my home use one account?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. Check the service's definitions of household and authorized user, credential-sharing rules, and any profile or device limits. Ask support if the terms do not address your household arrangement.

faqs.question: Does an offline download mean I can keep a permanent copy?
faqs.answer: No. Offline access is governed by the service's download and entitlement conditions and does not necessarily allow independent copying or continued access. Review the specific download terms for the title and membership.

faqs.question: Can I show subscription content at an event if I do not charge admission?
faqs.answer: Do not infer permission from whether money changes hands. Check the terms for public or group display and obtain explicit permission if the use is not clearly covered.

faqs.question: What if the help page and membership terms appear to disagree?
faqs.answer: Save the date and source of both statements and ask the service for a written clarification about your exact use. Avoid relying on the broader interpretation until the conflict is resolved.
